company.text: Miltenyi Biotec was founded in 1989 in Bergisch Gladbach (near Cologne) by **Stefan Miltenyi**, inventor of magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS). It sells tools across the cell-therapy workflow — sample prep, cell separation, flow cytometry, antibodies, cell culture media and **cytokines**, the CliniMACS Prodigy automated manufacturing platform — plus lentiviral-vector CDMO work through Lentigen in the US. Sites include a GMP plant in **Teterow** (Germany), North American HQ in **Gaithersburg, MD** (expanded 2022: manufacturing, R&D, QA, CDMO), and subsidiaries in about 28 countries. Acquisitions include Lentigen assets (2014), LaVision BioTec (2018) and biosensor maker **Lino Biotech** (Zurich, 2023). In 2026 it is converting a former pharma complex in **Cologne** (~12,000 m²) into a clinical-reagents plant, due online by end of 2026, and building a new €10M production hall in Teterow (groundbreaking Dec 2025).

financials.text: **Revenue:** not published by the company; third-party directories estimate **over $1B** (to be confirmed). **Employees:** ~4,600 worldwide (May 2026). **Funding:** none — founder-owned and self-financed; investing in capacity (Cologne clinical-reagents plant, Teterow €10M hall with 50–70 new jobs). Budget is not the issue; the barrier is **make-vs-buy** — they have internal protein capacity.

industry.title: Cell-therapy tools makers are adding capacity
industry.text: Miltenyi says demand for clinical reagents often exceeds supply — hence the Cologne and Teterow builds. Capacity strain inside a company is when outside expression partners get a call.

industry.title: Animal-free, GMP-grade proteins
industry.text: Cell-therapy customers push suppliers for animal-origin-free, GMP-ready cytokines and enzymes. Recombinant enzyme supply with clean documentation is a recurring buying criterion.

industry.title: Greener chemistry in pharma supply chains
industry.text: Pharma customers increasingly ask suppliers for lower-footprint processes; Miltenyi's own Cologne plant uses heat pumps to cut CO₂. Biocatalysis fits that same story.

talking_points: Which proteins or enzymes does your team still **buy outside** today, even with the internal protein group?
When the German protein group is fully booked, how do you handle **urgent or small-batch** expression needs?
Are there **difficult enzymes** (esterases, lipases, oxidoreductases) where an outside specialist would save time?
Do any of your products involve a **chemical synthesis step** that is costly or messy, where an enzyme could help?
Who in the protein group would be the right person to keep in the loop for niche requests?
